roles.name: Attorney under an enduring power of attorney (EPA)
roles.summary: Northern Ireland still uses EPAs, which cover property and financial affairs only. The attorney can act as soon as the EPA is signed, unless the document says otherwise. Once the donor is or is becoming mentally incapable, the attorney must apply to register it with the High Court (Office of Care and Protection). Until registration, the attorney's authority is suspended except for limited interim acts.

assigned.event: Donor executes an EPA in the prescribed form while capable

starts.event: On signing, unless the instrument sets conditions or restrictions on commencement

ends.event: Donor's incapacity supervenes: authority is suspended (apart from interim acts after applying) until the court registers the instrument
Death or bankruptcy of the donor, or death, incapacity or bankruptcy of the attorney: the court cancels registration
Revocation confirmed by the court, disclaimer notified to the court, or court cancels on fraud/undue pressure/unsuitability
Court exercises Part VIII Mental Health Order powers revoking the power (e.g. controller appointed)

states.label: Donor incapable; registration not yet complete
Application made; limited interim acts permitted
Registered by High Court (OCP); full authority

transitions.event: Attorney gives notices (Sch 1) and applies to High Court for registration
conditions: attorney must apply as soon as practicable once donor is or is becoming incapable

transitions.event: Attorney applies because donor is becoming incapable
High Court (Office of Care and Protection) registers instrument

conditions: common-law revocation of agency by death

transitions.event: Court confirms revocation, disclaimer notified, or registration cancelled/power revoked

notes.text: An EPA in NI covers financial matters only. There is no health and welfare equivalent in force.
Registration cancelled because the donor 'is and is likely to remain mentally capable' (art 10(4)(c)) does not revoke the power.

Lasting powers of attorney under the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 Part 5 remain prospective (not in operation) on legislation.gov.uk as of 16/17 Sept 2026. New EPAs therefore remain the only durable financial power available.

roles.name: Attorney under an ordinary (general) power of attorney
roles.summary: A non-enduring power of attorney stops working when the donor becomes mentally incapable of managing their affairs.

ends.event: Donor becomes mentally incapable of managing affairs

transitions.event: Donor dies (common-law end of agency; no NI primary source retrieved)

roles.name: Controller appointed by the High Court (Office of Care and Protection)
roles.summary: When the High Court is satisfied on medical evidence that a person is incapable, by reason of mental disorder, of managing their property and affairs, it may appoint a controller to act as it orders or authorises. Proceedings run through the Office of Care and Protection. A controller is discharged automatically on the patient's death.

assigned.event: High Court order appointing controller (interim powers possible pending determination)

starts.event: On the order, within the powers the court confers

ends.event: Death of the patient: discharged without any order
Court satisfied the patient has become capable: discharged by order
Court discharges at any time if expedient

conditions: medical evidence of incapacity by reason of mental disorder

notes.text: For low-value estates the OCP may make a short procedure order instead of appointing a controller.
When fully commenced, MCA (NI) 2016 Part 6 would replace this with court-appointed deputies (s 116) and repeal the Mental Health Order for people aged 16+. Those provisions are prospective.

NI has no court-appointed personal welfare decision maker (guardian-person equivalent) in operation for incapacity generally. Mental Health Order guardianship for mental disorder was not researched here.

roles.name: Executor (grant of probate)
roles.summary: The executor named in the will has first priority for a grant of probate from the Probate Office (High Court). The deceased's real and personal estate vests in the personal representatives. The executor should distribute as soon as reasonably practicable, and beneficiaries normally cannot sue for non-distribution within the first year.

starts.event: Executor's title derives from the will at death. Most asset holders require the grant of probate.

transitions.event: Testator dies; estate vests in personal representatives
Probate Office issues grant of probate

notes.text: The procedural rules for non-contentious probate in NI are in Rules of the Supreme Court (Northern Ireland) 1980 Order 97, as published by the Department of Justice. No separate 'Non-Contentious Probate Rules (NI) 1979' instrument was found on legislation.gov.uk.

roles.name: Administrator (letters of administration)
roles.summary: Where there is no will, or no executor able or willing to act, the Probate Office grants letters of administration in a statutory order of priority: surviving spouse, children or their issue, parents, siblings or their issue, then remoter kin. Before the grant, an intestate's estate vests in the Probate Judge.

assigned.event: Probate Office issues letters of administration to highest-priority applicant

conditions: priority: spouse; children/issue; parents; siblings/issue; then r 20(2) kin

notes.text: r 20(1)(i) as published reads 'surviving spouse'. Whether civil partners are added by later amendment was not verified in the DoJ reproduction.

roles.name: Person receiving a statutory small payment without a grant
roles.summary: Certain bodies can pay up to £20,000 on death without probate or other proof of title, to the person who appears entitled or to a nominee. These include co-operative and community benefit societies, credit unions and some public-sector superannuation schemes. Banks and building societies may also release small sums at their discretion.

assigned.event: Death (or earlier nomination by deceased where the scheme allows)

transitions.event: Claimant applies under a listed provision
conditions: not exceeding £20,000 (deaths after one month from 8 Dec 2020)

notes.text: nidirect says a grant may not be needed for about £20,000 or less in an account, but release by banks and insurers is discretionary and may require an indemnity. The statutory £20,000 limit applies only to the listed schemes.

roles.name: Nominated representative (Human Tissue Act 2004 s 4)
roles.summary: An adult may appoint one or more people to deal with consent to donation and other scheduled activities after their death. A nominated representative's consent takes priority over deemed consent and over family members.

assigned.event: Adult appoints orally before two witnesses, or in writing (witnessed, or in a will)

starts.event: On death, if the deceased left no decision of their own in force

ends.event: Consent given or refused, or representative not reasonably contactable in time (appointment disregarded)

transitions.event: Adult dies with no own decision in force
Not reasonably practicable to communicate in time; falls to deemed consent or qualifying relationship

roles.name: Person in a qualifying relationship (deemed consent regime)
roles.summary: Since the NI deemed-consent regime took effect in 2023, an adult who made no decision and appointed no representative is deemed to consent to transplantation, unless they are an excepted adult. The highest-ranked qualifying relative can block this only by giving information that would lead a reasonable person to conclude the deceased would not have consented. For excepted adults and non-transplant activities, that relative's consent is required.

assigned.event: By statute at death: ranking spouse/civil partner/partner; parent/child; sibling; grandparent/grandchild; sibling's child; step-parent; half-sibling; friend of long standing

starts.event: At death, where no own decision or nominated representative applies

ends.event: Consent given/refused, or deemed consent proceeds or is rebutted

transitions.event: Transplantation activity in NI for non-excepted adult: deemed consent applies
conditions: adult ordinarily resident in NI 12+ months and had capacity to understand deemed consent (s 3(9A))

transitions.event: Relative provides information that deceased would not have consented
No rebutting information; deemed consent stands
Excepted adult or non-transplant activity: highest-ranked relative consents or refuses

notes.text: Commencement dates conflict across sources. legislation.gov.uk and S.R. 2023/14 art 2 give 13 February 2023 for s 1 of the 2022 Act, but that Order's explanatory note says 5 April 2023. The Permitted Material Regulations (S.R. 2023/26) came into operation on 1 June 2023, and the Department of Health gives 1 June 2023 as the go-live date. This file uses 2023 and treats 1 June 2023 as the operative date.

roles.name: Executor or nearest surviving relative (disposal of remains)
roles.summary: NI has no statutory priority list for who controls disposal of a body. Cremation in Belfast requires an application by the executor or nearest surviving relative, or a satisfactory explanation why someone else is applying. Cremation is unlawful if the deceased left a written direction against it. Whoever arranges the funeral is responsible for the bill.

assigned.event: Executor named in will, or nearest surviving relative at death

ends.event: Burial or cremation completed (ashes notice to applicant/relative/executor)

transitions.event: Death; executor or nearest relative arranges
conditions: cremation barred if known written direction to the contrary

notes.text: UNVERIFIED: the executor's common-law right and duty to arrange disposal in NI. No NI primary judgment was retrieved, so the priority here rests only on the cremation application rule.
The 1961 Regulations were read in their as-made PDF form. Later amendments, for example after further crematoria opened, were not checked.

roles.name: Personal representative or claimant: access to a deceased patient's health records
localNames: person who may have a claim arising out of the patient's death
roles.summary: After a patient dies, their personal representative, or anyone who may have a claim arising from the death, may apply to the record holder for access. Access is refused if the patient asked for a note that they did not want this.

assigned.event: By statute on death (personal representative via will/grant; or claimant)

starts.event: On application to the holder after death

ends.event: Access given or refused (e.g. patient's note under art 6(3))

transitions.event: Holder gives access or copy within requisite period

notes.text: This is the NI counterpart of the Access to Health Records Act 1990, which covers Great Britain and is handled in the uk-national layer. Living patients' access is now under UK GDPR / DPA 2018.

poaDurableByDefault.note: An ordinary power of attorney ends on mental incapacity. Durability requires an EPA in prescribed form.

springingPoaAllowed.note: An EPA takes effect on signing unless the instrument sets conditions or restrictions on when it commences. This rests on DoJ guidance. Art 4 sets form requirements and does not prohibit commencement conditions.

poaRegistrationBeforeUse.note: No registration needed while the donor is capable. Once incapacity supervenes, authority is suspended until the High Court (OCP) registers the EPA, apart from limited interim acts.

healthAgentStartsOn.note: No health-care agent exists in operation. EPAs are financial only, and MCA (NI) 2016 LPAs are prospective. Treatment of an incapable adult is under common-law best interests, decided by the clinician; no-one can consent on the adult's behalf. The MCA (NI) 2016 s 9 protection-from-liability framework is in operation only for specified (deprivation of liberty) purposes.

supportedDecisionMakingStatute.name: Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 ss 1(4), 5 (principle; partly commenced)
supportedDecisionMakingStatute.note: MCA (NI) 2016 ss 1(4) and 5 require all practicable help and support before a person is treated as unable to decide. These are in operation only for Phase 1 purposes. There is no statutory supporter appointment.

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.note: No NI statute gives fiduciaries access to digital assets or accounts. Personal representatives take the estate generally under AEA (NI) 1955 s 1. This is absence-of-statute context; no search tool proves a negative.

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No NI statute recognises platform online tools.

organDonationModel.name: Human Tissue Act 2004 as amended by the Organ and Tissue Donation (Deemed Consent) Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 ('Dáithí's Law')
organDonationModel.note: Deemed consent for transplantation in NI (HTA 2004 s 3(6AA)), operative 1 June 2023. The commencement order's date conflicts with this; see the role note.

smallEstateWithoutGrant.note: Statutory limit of £20,000 for listed schemes (S.R. 2020/280). Banks may release similar sums at their discretion.

probateGrantName.note: Letters of administration (with or without will annexed) where there is no executor. Issued by the Probate Office of the High Court.

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: UK data protection covers living individuals only. The Access to Health Records (NI) Order 1993 art 5(1)(e) gives limited statutory access to deceased patients' records.

healthAgentPostDeathAuthority.note: No health agent exists. EPA registration is cancelled and a controller is discharged on death.

pendingLegislation.item: Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 - Part 5 lasting powers of attorney (s 97 ff), Part 6 deputies (s 116 ff), general care/treatment/personal welfare provisions, IMCAs, acts of restraint (s 12), and repeal of the Mental Health (NI) Order 1986 for 16+
pendingLegislation.status: enacted, not commenced (prospective on legislation.gov.uk as of 17 Sept 2026). Only Phase 1 (research 1.10.2019; deprivation of liberty and money & valuables 2.12.2019) is in operation. DoH NI (Sept 2024): no decisions on full implementation. Acts of restraint commencement was consulted on Sept-Dec 2024 but s 12 still shows as prospective.
